title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Advanced Adult Nursing Care
intro: Welcome to GNPS Program 5 - Advanced Adult Nursing Care. This program builds on the assessment and care-planning skills developed in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing I. The focus now moves to adults with acute, unstable or complex conditions that can deteriorate rapidly and require timely, coordinated nursing action. This level is designed around the higher-acuity adult-health capabilities expected within national nursing education programs. It introduces advanced assessment, emergency priorities, multiorgan risk and evidence-based nursing interventions while reinforcing the importance of practising within scope and escalating early. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Recognise high-risk adult medical-surgical conditions Apply ABC and safety-first frameworks in urgent situations Interpret important changes in vital signs and clinical findings Provide nursing care for cardiovascular and respiratory emergencies Respond to neurological, renal and endocrine deterioration Recognise sepsis, shock and multiorgan dysfunction Support safe use of emergency medicines and intravenous therapies Collaborate with the healthcare team during acute care Communicate clearly with patients and families during serious illness Complex illness may affect several body systems at once. A patient with sepsis may develop respiratory distress, hypotension, kidney injury and altered consciousness within a short period. Nurses need to recognise patterns, identify the immediate threat and act before deterioration becomes irreversible. By the end of Level 1, you should be able to recognise and respond safely to common high-acuity adult conditions, prioritise care and contribute effectively to emergency and multidisciplinary management.

content.text: Patients with complex conditions may show several abnormal findings at the same time. Advanced nursing assessment focuses on identifying the problem that threatens life or function first, while continuing to collect information about the whole clinical picture. Rapid assessment should be followed by focused reassessment after every intervention.
Learning outcomes
Perform a rapid ABC assessment Distinguish stable from unstable findings
Recognise clinical patterns suggesting deterioration Prioritise nursing actions in complex situations

Airway, Breathing and Circulation Airway obstruction, respiratory failure and circulatory collapse require immediate attention. The nurse should identify threats quickly, call for assistance and begin actions within scope while the emergency response is activated.

Clinical Trends One abnormal result may be less important than a worsening pattern. Increasing respiratory rate, falling blood pressure, reduced urine output, rising lactate or altered consciousness may indicate decompensation.

Expected and Unexpected Findings Expected findings are consistent with the condition or stage of recovery. Unexpected findings, such as sudden neurological change after surgery or new chest pain, require immediate reassessment and escalation.
Reassessment After oxygen, fluids, medication, positioning or other interventions, the nurse must reassess. Improvement, no change or worsening determines the next action.

Mr Kumar is admitted with pancreatitis. During the shift he becomes restless, tachycardic and hypotensive, and his urine output falls. The nurse recognises a pattern of circulatory compromise rather than treating each finding separately, initiates the deterioration pathway and prepares for urgent review.
Key learning points
Prioritise immediate threats before routine care Interpret combinations and trends, not isolated numbers
Treat unexpected changes as clinically significant Reassess after every intervention

Acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, pulmonary embolism, severe asthma, acute pulmonary oedema and respiratory failure can deteriorate rapidly. Nursing care focuses on early recognition, oxygenation, circulation, monitoring and timely escalation.
Learning outcomes
Recognise common cardiac and respiratory emergencies Identify signs of haemodynamic and respiratory compromise
Implement immediate evidence-based nursing actions Monitor response and anticipate complications

Acute Coronary Syndrome Chest pressure, diaphoresis, nausea, breathlessness or ECG change may indicate myocardial ischaemia. Immediate assessment, cardiac monitoring, prescribed emergency treatment and rapid escalation are essential.

Arrhythmias and Heart Failure Fast, slow or irregular rhythms may reduce cardiac output. Acute heart failure may cause breathlessness, crackles, hypoxia and fluid overload. Nurses monitor rhythm, perfusion, oxygenation and response to therapy.

Pulmonary Embolism and ARDS Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia or tachycardia may suggest pulmonary embolism. ARDS produces severe oxygenation failure. Both require urgent multidisciplinary management.

Severe Asthma and Respiratory Failure Inability to speak, silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness or worsening blood gases indicate severe risk. The nurse should escalate immediately and support emergency airway and breathing care.

A patient being treated for asthma becomes quieter, with reduced air entry and increasing drowsiness. Although wheezing has decreased, the nurse recognises that this may indicate exhaustion rather than improvement and activates urgent medical review.
Key learning points
Reduced symptoms do not always mean improvement Monitor perfusion as well as heart rhythm
Escalate sudden breathlessness or chest pain urgently Recognise fatigue and altered consciousness as late respiratory signs

Neurological, renal and endocrine emergencies can produce rapid changes in consciousness, circulation and electrolyte balance. Nurses need to recognise red flags, protect the patient from immediate harm and support targeted treatment.
Learning outcomes
Recognise signs of stroke, seizure and raised intracranial pressure Identify acute kidney injury and dangerous electrolyte changes
Recognise diabetic and thyroid emergencies Implement immediate safety and monitoring measures

Stroke and Seizures Sudden facial weakness, speech difficulty, limb weakness or visual change may indicate stroke. During a seizure, protect the airway and patient from injury, time the event and observe recovery.

Raised Intracranial Pressure Declining consciousness, vomiting, unequal pupils, severe headache or abnormal vital-sign patterns may indicate increased intracranial pressure. Avoid delays in escalation.

Renal and Electrolyte Emergencies Acute kidney injury may present with reduced urine output, fluid overload, acidosis or electrolyte disturbance. Severe potassium, sodium or calcium changes can affect cardiac and neurological function.

Endocrine Emergencies DKA and HHS cause dehydration and metabolic instability. Thyroid storm and myxoedema coma can be life-threatening. Nurses monitor glucose, fluids, electrolytes, temperature, consciousness and treatment response.

A patient with diabetes develops deep rapid breathing, abdominal pain, dehydration and increasing drowsiness. The nurse suspects diabetic ketoacidosis, checks glucose and ketones, begins the emergency pathway and monitors fluid, electrolyte and neurological status.
Key learning points
Treat sudden neurological change as an emergency Monitor urine output as a key indicator of perfusion
Recognise that electrolyte changes can cause arrhythmias Follow emergency protocols while reassessing continuously

Sepsis and shock can progress to multiorgan failure. Early recognition and rapid treatment improve outcomes. Nurses are often the first to recognise the combination of infection, altered perfusion and organ dysfunction.
Learning outcomes
Recognise early sepsis and shock Differentiate common patterns of circulatory failure
Support time-critical interventions Monitor for organ dysfunction and treatment response
Sepsis Recognition Possible infection combined with new confusion, rapid breathing, hypotension, fever or hypothermia, reduced urine output or rising lactate requires urgent assessment.
Shock may be hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive or obstructive. Common signs include altered consciousness, poor skin perfusion, tachycardia, hypotension and reduced urine output.

Time-Critical Care Emergency pathways may include cultures, antimicrobial therapy, oxygen, intravenous access, fluids and lactate measurement. Nurses should follow local protocols and monitor carefully.

Multiorgan Dysfunction Worsening respiratory, renal, cardiovascular, hepatic or neurological function indicates severe illness. Accurate documentation and trend communication support coordinated care.

Ms Lee has a urinary infection and becomes confused, tachypnoeic and hypotensive. The nurse recognises sepsis with possible shock, activates the emergency pathway, obtains observations and specimens as directed, supports immediate treatment and monitors response closely.
Key learning points
Act on suspected sepsis before severe collapse Use perfusion and organ-function indicators together
Follow time-critical pathways accurately Communicate trends and treatment response clearly

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 5 - Level 1, you have developed essential skills in advanced assessment, urgent prioritisation and nursing care for common high-acuity adult conditions. These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to complex interpretation, high-risk therapies and international acute-care practice.
